content.text: I fixed the bug in `solution/core.py`, and both visible tests now pass. When `merge` combined an interval into the previous one, it set the new end to the incoming interval's end (`out[-1] = (pa, b)`) instead of the larger of the two ends. Since the input is only sorted by start, any interval that sits inside an earlier one, like `(2, 3)` inside `(1, 4)` or the point `(2, 2)` inside `(1, 3)`, made the merged interval shorter and cut off the rest of the containing one. The fix is to use `max(pb, b)` as the merged end, which keeps the outer interval whole however its contained intervals are ordered. I also ran a few extra cases by hand: an interval holding several smaller ones, a nested interval that touches a later one, and touching intervals with `join_touching` on and off. All gave the expected results.

When `merge` combined an interval into the previous one, it set the new end to the incoming interval's end (`out[-1] = (pa, b)`) instead of the larger of the two ends. Since the input is only sorted by start, any interval that sits inside an earlier one, like `(2, 3)` inside `(1, 4)` or the point `(2, 2)` inside `(1, 3)`, made the merged interval shorter and cut off the rest of the containing one. The fix is to use `max(pb, b)` as the merged end, which keeps the outer interval whole however its contained intervals are ordered. I also ran a few extra cases by hand: an interval holding several smaller ones, a nested interval that touches a later one, and touching intervals with `join_touching` on and off. All gave the expected results.
